title: Net Zero transition brings opportunity to build, not just import, technology
where: Editorial page, page 8 (Ramakrishna R Sonde, professor emeritus, BITS Pilani & Goa)
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: indigenization of technology and developing new technology · GS3 › Industrial policy · GS3 › Climate change and energy transition
summary: India struggles to take research from the laboratory to industry; the author argues the Net Zero transition is a chance to build Indian technology by sharing development risk among government, academia and industry.
ideas: Atmanirbharta is more than assembly: manufacturing equipment while importing process know-how, materials, catalysts, designs and IP creates jobs but not technological independence.
GS3 · Indigenisation of technology
True atmanirbharta means owning the know-why and IP, not just assembling imported designs.
The 'valley of death': Indian academia works up to about TRL 3–4 while industry enters around TRL 7; the gap between lab validation and industrial demonstration is underfunded.
GS3 · R&D and innovation
Ideas die between TRL 4 and TRL 7, where neither academia nor industry is willing to pay.
Five recurring reasons: technology takes time and patient capital; industry wants proven technology; scale-up is complex; collaboration is weak; and nobody owns the journey.
GS3 · Innovation ecosystem
Technology development stalls because no one owns the journey from lab to plant.
Shared risk: government should carry more early-stage risk, industry's share should rise as uncertainty falls; deep-tech incubators and demonstration centres can bridge the gap.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Sharing development risk, with government taking the earliest bets, is how a new Indian technology gets proven.

Net Zero as an opening: green hydrogen, carbon capture, storage, sustainable fuels and circular manufacturing will reshape steel, cement, chemicals, fertilisers, transport and power; India can build new plants on new processes.
GS3 · Energy transition / industry
As India builds new steel, cement and fertiliser plants, it can build them on Indian technology rather than imported designs.
keywords: Technology readiness level (TRL)
A nine-stage scale from basic idea to proven commercial deployment
GS3 · S&T
Indian research stalls between TRL 4 and TRL 7, the stage of pilots and demonstration plants.
Know-how vs know-why
Knowing how to run a technology vs understanding why it works, which enables IP
GS3 · Indigenisation
Moving from know-how to know-why is what turns a manufacturer into a technology owner.
Patient capital
Long-horizon funding that accepts delays and failure
GS3 · Investment models
Deep-tech needs patient capital, which is why the state must share early risk.
Technology denial
Restrictions by other countries on access to advanced technology
GS3 · Strategic technology
Technology denial pushed India's atomic programme to build its own capabilities.
examples: India's atomic energy programme
Facing technology denial, India built its own capabilities through scientific leadership, freedom for scientists and acceptance of failure
GS4
GS3 · Indigenisation · GS4 · Leadership
The atomic programme shows that scientific leadership and tolerance of failure build indigenous technology.
Coal gasification for high-ash coal
Needs resources and commitment far beyond a successful R&D pilot plant
GS3 · Energy technology
Coal gasification suited to India's high-ash coal shows how scale-up, not invention, is the bottleneck.
pyqs: Energy independence by 2047 through clean technology.

trend.t: Science and technology questions have turned from general achievements to strategic indigenisation: the Semiconductor Mission, PLI and CCUS (all 2025) and energy independence through clean technology (2025).
trend.watch: Four 2025 questions touched indigenous technology for industry and energy, so the lab-to-industry gap and Atmanirbhar Bharat in clean technology are strong areas for the next paper.
focus: Lessons from atomic and space programmes

potential: "India must not settle for becoming merely a large market for technologies developed elsewhere." Discuss in the context of the Net Zero transition. (15 marks)

title: AI has made Taiwan the world's fastest growing large economy
syllabus: GS3 › Growth and development; investment models · GS3 › Industrial policy (semiconductors) · GS3 › Science and technology (AI)
summary: Taiwan's GDP grew 14.36% in July–September 2026, driven by AI-linked investment and chip exports led by TSMC, overtaking India as the fastest growing large economy this year.
ideas: Investment-led boom: investments rose 26.36% year-on-year and accounted for almost half of Taiwan's 14.36% Q3 growth; investment and exports together explained almost 80%.
GS3 · Growth / investment
Taiwan's AI boom is investment-led: capital spending explains half its record growth.
One firm, one nation: TSMC, the world's largest chip manufacturer, was estimated to account for nearly a tenth of Taiwan's GDP; its 2026 revenue is seen at $175 billion, 43% higher.
GS3 · Semiconductors / industrial policy
TSMC alone is about a tenth of Taiwan's GDP, showing the value of owning a strategic technology.
Spillover: OCBC notes the AI upcycle is spilling from exports into local equipment spending and capacity expansion; South Korea and the US also posted strong AI-driven growth.
GS3 · Global value chains
The AI boom rewards economies that sit inside the hardware value chain.
For India: India's GDP grew 8.6% and 7.8% in the first two quarters of 2026; Indian markets were 'largely bypassed by the AI investment boom' (front page, p. 2).
GS3 · India's growth strategy
India grows fast on domestic demand, but Taiwan shows the premium of being in the AI hardware chain.
keywords: Investment-led growth
Growth driven by capital spending rather than consumption
GS3 · Macroeconomy
Taiwan's 2026 surge is a textbook case of investment-led growth.
Concentration risk
Dependence of an economy on one firm or sector
GS3 · Economic resilience
A tenth of GDP from one company brings growth and concentration risk.
data: Taiwan's real GDP growth, July–September 2026
Taiwan's Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics
GS3 · Comparative growth
Taiwan's GDP grew 14.36% in July–September 2026 on the back of AI investment.
examples: TSMC
World's largest chip maker, central to the global AI investment boom
GS3 · Semiconductor strategy
TSMC shows why India's Semiconductor Mission aims at chip making, not just assembly.

trend.t: Industrial policy questions moved from Make in India (2015) to manufacturing's share (2023) and, in 2025, PLI and the Semiconductor Mission.
trend.watch: Semiconductors and PLI were both asked in 2025, so comparative examples like Taiwan and South Korea are useful.
focus: Global value chains in AI hardware

potential: What lessons can India draw from Taiwan's semiconductor-led growth for its own industrial policy? (10 marks)

title: Cabinet clears Rs 2,814-cr critical mineral processing scheme and Rs 17,500-cr energy storage scheme
where: Economy, page 13 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box on energy storage
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Industrial policy; Investment models (viability gap funding) · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources (critical minerals) · GS2 › Government policies and interventions
summary: The Cabinet approved a Rs 2,814-crore capex scheme (30% capital subsidy) for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, and a Rs 17,500-crore viability gap funding scheme for 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage.
evolution: To ease the energy transition, ramp up storage and strengthen transmission.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal for the next 10–11 years.
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: Processing is the chokepoint: India has little processing capacity and is almost 100% import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon, while China dominates processing and uses it as leverage in trade tensions.
GS3 · Mineral security / GS2 · Strategic vulnerability
Mining alone is not enough: control of processing decides who holds leverage in the critical mineral value chain.

Targeted capex support: a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium plants (30 kt each) and two nickel plants (50 kt each), capped at Rs 500 crore and Rs 900 crore per beneficiary, serving EVs, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for lithium and nickel plants aim to build the missing middle of India's battery value chain.

Mineral-specific parks: Gujarat (heavy rare earths) and Andhra Pradesh (a rare earth corridor), Odisha for nickel (reserves, and an eastern location for imports from Indonesia), Maharashtra for lithium, each as a complete ecosystem; a stockpiling policy is also being drafted.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Mineral security
Siting each processing park where reserves, skills or import routes exist applies the logic of resource-based industrial location.

Storage closes the renewable gap: Rs 17,500 crore (2026-27 to 2030-31) for 92 GWh (30 GWh battery storage, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh emerging technologies), equal to 170% of existing grid-scale capacity, because renewable power is abundant in some hours and short in others.
GS3 · Energy infrastructure
Energy storage turns intermittent solar and wind into dependable power, the missing link of India's transition.

Market design plus Make in India: storage capacity will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding, discoms are eligible for VGF, and battery projects must meet a 40% domestic content requirement, linking storage demand to domestic manufacturing.
GS3 · Investment models (VGF) / Make in India
Viability gap funding with competitive bidding and domestic content rules uses public money to crowd in private investment and local manufacturing.
keywords: Viability Gap Funding (VGF)
A capital grant that makes a socially needed but commercially weak project viable
GS3 · Investment models
VGF for storage bridges the gap between high upfront costs and affordable tariffs.
Pumped hydro storage
Pumping water uphill with surplus power and releasing it through turbines at peak demand
GS3 · Energy
Pumped hydro, two-thirds of the new storage target, is an old technology with a new role in the energy transition.
Domestic Content Requirement (DCR)
A rule that a share of a project's components be made in India
GS3 · Industrial policy
A 40% DCR ties battery storage demand to India's own manufacturing base.
Strategic stockpile
A reserve of critical minerals to guard against supply disruptions
GS3 · Mineral security
A critical mineral stockpile does for batteries what strategic petroleum reserves do for oil.
Intermittency
Variability of solar and wind output across hours and seasons
GS3 · Renewable energy
Storage is the answer to intermittency, which grows with every gigawatt of solar added.
data: 54 GWh now; 411 GWh target by 2031-32
India's grid-scale energy storage capacity and its target
Government of India (Union Cabinet), via IE
GS3 · Energy storage
India has about 54 GWh of grid-scale storage against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32: a near eightfold scale-up is needed.
examples: Odisha chosen for nickel processing
Domestic reserves plus an eastern location to process nickel imported from Indonesia
GS1 · Industrial location · GS3 · Mineral security
Odisha's nickel park shows industrial location balancing local resources with access to imported ore.
Storage VGF scheme (92 GWh)
30 GWh batteries, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh new technologies
GS3 · Energy transition · Investment models
The Rs 17,500-crore storage VGF is a ready example of public funds crowding in about Rs 97,600 crore of investment.
pyqs: Key challenges to India's energy security; measures with growth and sustainability.
Will India meet 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030? Role of shifting subsidies.
Status and targets for renewable energy; National Programme on LEDs.
Can regional resource-based manufacturing promote employment in India?
Multi-dimensional implications of the uneven distribution of mineral oil in the world.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and solar costs (2015, 2016) to whether India can meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and, in 2026, energy security with growth and sustainability. Mineral questions so far asked about the distribution of resources (2021) and the environmental hazards of mining (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in 2026 (GS3) and 2025 (GS2), so it is a must-study area. The next step is likely the transition's own dependencies: storage, grids and critical minerals.
focus: Storage and grid integration of renewables
Critical mineral value chains and dependence on China
Investment models for clean energy (VGF, PLI, competitive bidding)

potential: "Energy storage is the missing link in India's renewable energy transition." Discuss. (10 marks)
Why is processing, rather than mining, the weakest link in India's critical mineral value chain? Examine the steps taken to address it. (15 marks)
What is viability gap funding? Explain its role in promoting grid-scale energy storage in India. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Energy storage is the missing link in India's renewable energy transition." Discuss.
parts: Why storage is the missing link

answer.t: In November 2026 the Cabinet approved Rs 17,500 crore of viability gap funding for 92 GWh of storage, as India has only about 54 GWh against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32.

answer.h: Why storage is the missing link

pts.t: Solar and wind are abundant in some hours and short in others, so supply must be shifted in time.
pts.ex: Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks in the evening.

pts.t: Storage balances sudden swings in renewable output.
pts.ex: Sri Lanka's 2026 blackout from rooftop solar disconnecting (IE, 4 Nov 2026).

pts.t: Surplus renewable power can be stored instead of wasted.
Stored power can meet evening peaks now met by thermal plants.
Storage makes the 500 GW non-fossil target usable round the clock.
pts.ex: PM's 500 GW goal (Nov 2026).

pts.t: Battery demand can anchor domestic manufacturing.
pts.ex: 40% domestic content rule for battery projects.

pts.t: Storage projects are capital-heavy, so tariffs are high without support.
Batteries need lithium and nickel that India imports almost entirely.
Financially stressed utilities struggle to pay for storage.
Sites, land and environmental clearances take time.
Few markets yet reward storage for balancing services.
Competitive bidding with capital support.
pts.ex: 92 GWh VGF scheme.

pts.t: Processing capacity and stockpiles.
pts.ex: Rs 2,814-crore processing scheme; NCMM stockpile.

pts.t: Batteries for short duration, pumped hydro for longer.
Pay for ancillary and balancing services.
Recover battery minerals to reduce import needs.

answer.t: Adding solar and wind builds India's clean power; storage makes it dependable, so the transition will move only as fast as storage does.

title: Tamil Nadu tightens grip on women-led electronics manufacturing
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Population and migration · GS3 › Employment; Industrial policy (manufacturing) · GS2 › Welfare of vulnerable sections; best practices in governance · GS4 › Innovation in public service; gender justice
summary: Annual Survey of Industries data for 2024-25 show Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India and 44.4% of those making computer, electronic and optical products, helped by dormitories near factories.
evolution: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses (women and work thread).
Physicists bring STEM to women and rural youth.
ideas: Concentration of women's factory work: Tamil Nadu's share of directly employed women making computer, electronic and optical products rose from 42.9% to 44.4% in 2024-25; it employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India.
GS1 · Women and work / GS3 · Manufacturing
Tamil Nadu employs two in five of India's directly employed women factory workers: proof that state policy shapes women's work.

A policy innovation that removes the real barriers: the two key obstacles for women are distance from work and living arrangements, and Tamil Nadu adapted China's model of dormitories for women workers.
GS4 · Innovation in public service / GS2 · Best practices
Tamil Nadu's factory dormitories are an innovation that solves women's real constraints, safety and distance, rather than offering only jobs.

Migration and an ageing south: southern states with ageing populations rely on migrant workers, so housing near factories is a key policy intervention; most surveyed migrants in the Chennai region came from Bihar, Odisha, Assam, UP and Jharkhand.
GS1 · Migration and demography
As the south ages and draws migrant workers from the east, worker housing becomes core industrial infrastructure.

A wide gender gap remains: directly employed women factory workers rose by 96,907 to 17.38 lakh, while men rose by 4.54 lakh to 78.78 lakh; Gujarat's share of women in electronics fell from 10% to 7.4%.
GS1 · Gender gap / GS3 · Employment
Women remain a small minority of India's factory workforce, so gains in one state must spread nationally.
A blind spot in the data: the survey gives no gender break-up of 70.31 lakh contract workers, so the true number of women in factories cannot be known.
GS3 · Employment data / GS2 · Statistics
Without gender data on contract workers, policy for women in factories is made half-blind.
keywords: Enabling infrastructure
Housing, transport, safety and childcare that let women take up jobs
GS1 · Women / GS3 · Employment
Enabling infrastructure, not just job creation, decides whether women join the factory workforce.
Policy transfer
Adapting a policy that worked elsewhere to local conditions
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Innovation
Tamil Nadu's dormitory model is policy transfer done well: borrowing the idea, adapting it to local needs.
Feminisation of manufacturing
Rising share of women in factory work, as in East Asian electronics
GS1 · Women / GS3 · Industry
Electronics assembly can drive the feminisation of Indian manufacturing, as it did in East Asia.
Gender-disaggregated data
Statistics broken down by sex to show gaps
GS2 · Statistics / GS1 · Gender
Gender-disaggregated data on contract workers is the first step to gender-responsive labour policy.
Contractualisation
Growing use of contract rather than directly employed workers
GS3 · Labour
Contractualisation hides women workers from the statistics and from labour protections.
data: Tamil Nadu's share of all directly employed women factory workers in India, 2024-25
Annual Survey of Industries 2024-25 (MoSPI)
GS1 · Women and work / GS3 · Manufacturing
Tamil Nadu alone employs 40.3% of India's directly employed women factory workers (ASI 2024-25).
17.38 lakh women vs 78.78 lakh men
Directly employed factory workers in India, 2024-25
Annual Survey of Industries 2024-25 (MoSPI)
GS1 · Gender gap / GS3 · Employment
India's factories directly employ 17.38 lakh women against 78.78 lakh men (ASI 2024-25): a stark gender gap.
examples: Tamil Nadu's dormitories for women workers
Housing near factories, adapted from China's model
GS4
GS1 · Women · GS3 · Jobs · GS4 · Innovation in public service · Essay
Tamil Nadu's dormitory model shows how a simple, innovative idea can unlock women's participation in manufacturing.
Gujarat's falling share in women's electronics jobs
From 10% to 7.4% as women's direct jobs there fell
GS3 · Industrial policy · GS2 · Cooperative and competitive federalism
Gujarat's falling share against Tamil Nadu's rise shows states competing on policy design, not just incentives.
pyqs: Gender equality, equity and empowerment; gender concerns in programme design.
Urban migration of skilled, young, unmarried women and their freedom and family ties.
Continued challenges for women in India against time and space.
How patriarchy affects the middle-class working woman.
Care economy vs monetised economy; bringing care into the monetised economy.
Manufacturing's share in GDP, especially MSMEs; present policies.
A public official needs innovativeness and creativity to resolve ethical dilemmas.

trend.t: Women questions moved from patriarchy and the working woman (2014) and globalisation's effects (2015) to challenges of 'time and space' (2019), the gig economy (2021), the care economy (2023) and gender concerns in programme design and women's migration (2024).
trend.watch: Women and work have been asked almost every year, so this is a must-study area. Questions now ask about the conditions that shape women's work, such as space, safety, care and migration, more than about the jobs themselves.
focus: Barriers to women's work: safety, mobility, care, housing
Women in manufacturing and services; migration

potential: "Women's participation in manufacturing depends as much on enabling infrastructure as on jobs." Discuss with reference to Tamil Nadu. (15 marks)
Why does India's female labour force participation remain low despite economic growth? Suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Women's participation in manufacturing depends as much on enabling infrastructure as on jobs." Discuss with reference to Tamil Nadu.

answer.t: The Annual Survey of Industries 2024-25 shows Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of India's directly employed women factory workers, helped by dormitories that address distance and housing.

pts.t: Dormitories near factories let women, including migrants, take jobs far from home.
pts.ex: Tamil Nadu's dormitory model adapted from China.

pts.t: Safe housing and transport reassure women and their families.
Less commuting frees time and money.
Young women from other states can move for work.
pts.ex: Migrant workers in the Chennai region from Bihar, Odisha, Assam, UP and Jharkhand.

pts.t: Firms needing large women workforces cluster where housing exists.
pts.ex: Tamil Nadu's 44.4% share of women in electronics manufacturing.

pts.t: Solving women's real constraints rather than only offering incentives is innovation in public service.
Patriarchal norms and family restrictions limit women's mobility.
Unpaid care work keeps many women out of full-time jobs.
Contract work, low wages and long hours deter women.
pts.ex: 70.31 lakh contract workers without gender data.

pts.t: Limited technical training restricts women to low-skill roles.
Strict rules can curb personal freedom.
Gains concentrate in a few states.
pts.ex: Gujarat's share fell from 10% to 7.4%.

pts.t: Industry-government partnerships for women's hostels near clusters.
pts.ex: Working women hostels announced in Budget 2024-25.

pts.t: Creches and buses at industrial parks.
Night shifts with consent and safety, equal pay and grievance redress.
Train women for higher-skill electronics roles.
Gender break-up of contract workers in the ASI.
pts.ex: VISTAR statistics scheme (2026).

pts.t: Let other states adopt Tamil Nadu's model.

answer.t: Jobs open the factory door, but housing, safety and care let women walk through it; Tamil Nadu shows that a simple idea can turn women's potential into India's manufacturing strength.

title: Bengal's new industry policy thinks outside the box: Pooling land to taking back unused land
syllabus: GS3 › Land reforms; Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Investment models · GS2 › Government policies and interventions (state); e-governance and transparency · GS4 › Fairness and transparency in land allotment
summary: West Bengal's Investment Promotion Policy, 2026 proposes direct purchase of land, land pooling and taking back unused industrial land, with production required within three years of allotment.
ideas: Land is the binding constraint: large contiguous plots are not available as land is fragmented into small holdings, so pooling is proposed to create large areas for major industries.
GS3 · Land reforms / industrial policy
Fragmented holdings make land the main bottleneck to industry, which land pooling seeks to solve.
Consent over coercion: the state wants to buy land directly rather than acquire it ('We do not want another Singur or Nandigram'), learning from the movements that ended the Left Front's rule.
GS3 · Land acquisition / GS2 · Governance
Bengal's shift from acquisition to purchase and pooling reflects the political lesson of Singur and Nandigram: consent sustains industry.
Use it or lose it: production must begin within three years of allotment, land cannot be used for other purposes, unused industrial land will be recovered, and brownfield redevelopment gets priority.
GS3 · Efficient use of land
A three-year 'use it or lose it' clause stops land hoarding by investors.

Transparency by design: a GIS-enabled inventory of industrial land (ownership, plot size, use, connectivity, utilities, encumbrances), published criteria, online applications, time-stamped scrutiny and disclosure of decisions.
GS2 · E-governance and transparency
A GIS land inventory with online, time-stamped allotment cuts discretion and the scope for corruption.

Safeguards and inclusion: land support does not exempt units from land-use, environment, rehabilitation, tenancy, forest or coastal laws; the policy favours labour-intensive industries and MSMEs employing more women and transgender people. Pooling terms are yet to be detailed.
GS3 · Inclusive industrialisation
Land support must not bypass rehabilitation and environmental law, or today's investment becomes tomorrow's Singur.
keywords: Land pooling
Landowners pool plots for development and get back a share of developed land or benefits
GS3 · Land policy
Land pooling makes landowners partners in development rather than displaced sellers.
Brownfield redevelopment
Reusing previously developed or idle industrial land
GS3 · Industry / land use
Brownfield redevelopment brings industry without taking new farmland.
Land bank
A government-maintained inventory of land ready for allotment
GS3 · Investment climate
A GIS land bank cuts the time investors spend searching for land.
Use-it-or-lose-it clause
A condition that allotted land must be used within a set time or be taken back
GS3 · Efficient land use
Use-it-or-lose-it clauses turn allotted land into factories, not speculation.
examples: 'No more Singur or Nandigram'
Bengal shifts from acquisition to direct purchase and pooling
GS4
GS3 · Land acquisition · GS4 · Consent and fairness
Singur and Nandigram remain India's lesson that industry built without consent cannot last.
GIS-enabled industrial land inventory
Online, time-stamped allotment with disclosed decisions
GS4
GS2 · E-governance · GS4 · Transparency
A public, GIS-based land inventory is an example of technology reducing discretion in allotment.
pyqs: Key issues addressed by the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
Why industrial growth lagged GDP after reforms; can recent industrial policy changes help?
Manufacturing's share in GDP, especially MSMEs; present policies.
Drafting a fair compensation-cum-rehabilitation policy for persons displaced by projects.

trend.t: Land questions have tested the 2013 land acquisition law (2014) and, repeatedly, land reforms in agriculture (2013, 2016, 2021, 2023, 2024). Industrial policy questions asked why manufacturing lags (2017, 2023). GS4 asked for a fair rehabilitation policy (2016).
trend.watch: Land reforms recur most years in GS3, so land is a must-study area; questions on land for industry, consent and rehabilitation can draw on new state policies such as pooling.
focus: Land acquisition vs land pooling vs direct purchase
Land as a constraint on manufacturing

potential: "Land pooling is a more democratic alternative to land acquisition." Critically examine. (10 marks)

title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Mid-stream processing
Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
GS3 · Industry
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Weaponisation of supply chains
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
GS2 · IR / GS3 · Economy
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
Strategic stockpile
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
GS3 · Economy / Security
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Value-chain localisation
Building each stage of production at home
GS3 · Industrial policy
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Resource-based clusters
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
GS1 · Location of industries
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Rs 500 crore
Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
GS3 · Mineral security
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.
China's leverage over mineral processing
Dominance used as leverage in trade tensions
GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.
Why India's mining contributes little to GDP despite its Gondwana origin.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

potential: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains. (15 marks)
Why has India remained import-dependent for critical minerals despite its resource base? Examine the role of processing capacity. (10 marks)

title: Companies may be selective, but pvt capex picking up: FM
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: growth, development and employment; Industrial policy (MSMEs, PLI); Investment · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Governance · GS4 › Trust and public service values in governance
summary: The Finance Minister said private investment is picking up selectively after the GST 2.0 reforms, MSMEs are being helped to grow through a new definition, and the PLI scheme's weaker sectors will be examined, with trust in citizens as the government's charter.

A broad base of MSMEs and startups, not a few conglomerates, makes growth inclusive and resilient.

A trust-based state treats citizens as partners, cutting compliance burden and building cooperation.

MSMEs account for about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister), so their growth is export growth.

answer.t: MSMEs produce about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister, Nov 2026), yet most stay micro; the government says it wants micro firms to grow into small, medium and large ones.

pts.t: Firms lose subsidies, reservations and tax benefits once they cross size limits, so they stay small.
pts.ex: The revised definition aims to remove this.

pts.t: Lack of collateral and formal records limits access to bank loans.
Large buyers and governments pay late, choking working capital.
Many inspections, filings and licences cost more for small firms.

pts.t: Old machines and untrained workers keep productivity low.
Many firms stay outside the formal system to avoid tax and regulation.
Tiny firms cannot reach economies of scale.
Most employment is informal and low-paid.
pts.ex: Link: 'the challenge is wages, not jobs' (IE, 2 Nov).

pts.t: Few firms are large enough to supply global value chains.
A few large groups dominate while the base stays weak.

answer.h: Measures to help them scale up

pts.t: Let firms keep benefits for a period after crossing thresholds.
pts.ex: Revised MSME definition.

pts.t: Lend on digital transaction records, not just collateral.
pts.ex: TReDS for invoice discounting; CGTMSE credit guarantees.

pts.t: Penalise late payments to MSMEs.
Self-certification, fewer inspections, decriminalised minor offences.
pts.ex: FM: policy built on trusting business.

pts.t: Common facilities, testing labs and tool rooms for MSME clusters.

pts.k: Link to big firms and PLI
pts.t: Bring MSMEs into supply chains of large manufacturers and incentive schemes.
pts.ex: PLI rewards additional production.

pts.t: Apprenticeships and easy registration bring firms into the formal economy.
pts.ex: Udyam registration.

answer.t: India will become a manufacturing power only when its micro firms are free and able to grow; trust, credit and a growth-friendly policy can fill the missing middle.

title: The challenge is more productive employment
syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment; Growth and development · GS1 › Poverty; Role of women; Migration · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty
summary: With extreme poverty down to 2.6%, the editorial argues the next obstacle to mass prosperity is the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023; poverty concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt (front page).
Manish Sabharwal: 'Challenge is wages, not jobs' (editorial page).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
ideas: Poverty fell, productivity did not follow: extreme poverty is down to 2.6% and the $4.2 line to 16.1%, but the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs now blocks mass prosperity.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
India's next development challenge is not poverty reduction alone but productive employment.
More workers, not better work: labour force participation has risen, mostly as women join, but many are in farming or self-employment.
GS3 · Employment / GS1 · Women
Rising participation driven by women in farm and self-employment adds workers without raising productivity.
Stalled structural transformation: agriculture still employs a large share of workers compared with China and Vietnam, and most non-farm workers are in informal, low-productivity firms.
GS3 · Structural transformation
India's workforce has not moved out of farming at the pace East Asian economies managed.
Manufacturing missed its role: unlike other Asian economies, Indian manufacturing has not absorbed low-skilled workers; jobs grew in low-end services instead.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Without labour-intensive manufacturing, workers leaving farms crowd into low-end services.
Geography of jobs: poverty is concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt, where incomes and jobs are scarce, so migration to richer regions is the main route to non-farm work.
GS1 · Migration / Regional disparity
Regional job deserts make migration the default escape route from poverty.

answer.t: Extreme poverty is down to 2.6% (World Bank), yet only 21.68% of China's and 25% of Vietnam's workers are in farming, far below India, because Indian manufacturing has not absorbed surplus labour.

title: Energy security depends on if we electrify, and how we do it
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Neha Dhingra, CLASP)
syllabus: GS3 › Energy infrastructure; Conservation; Industrial policy (MSMEs) · GS2 › Energy security and foreign policy; Statutory bodies (BEE, BIS) · GS1 › Effects of globalisation on Indian society · GS4 › Innovation in public service
summary: After the Hormuz disruption hit India's LPG supply, the writer argues that electrifying industrial heat (heat pumps) and kitchens (induction) cuts import exposure, if standards and domestic supply come first.
ideas: A far-off war reached Indian kitchens: when Hormuz shipping stalled in March, families queued for cooking gas; the writer notes India imports about 60% of its LPG, nearly 90% of it via the strait.
GS2 · Energy security / GS1 · Globalisation
India's LPG dependence on one chokepoint shows how a distant conflict becomes a domestic crisis within weeks.

Electrification is a security strategy: in NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario, electricity's share of final energy rises from 21% to 60% by 2070 and the fuel import bill falls from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%.
GS3 · Energy transition
Electrification turns India's clean power base into energy security by replacing imported fuel with domestic electricity.

Industrial heat is the lowest-hanging fruit: factories burn coal, oil and gas on site for much of their energy; electrifying it cuts imports, decarbonises industry and helps exporters meet the EU's CBAM.
GS3 · Industry / Climate
Electrifying industrial heat cuts fuel imports, decarbonises industry and protects exports from carbon border taxes.

How we electrify matters: a heat pump, an air conditioner in reverse, gives 2.5 to 4 units of heat per unit of electricity against at most one from an electric boiler; much MSME heat is below 250°C, within its range.
GS3 · Energy efficiency / MSMEs
Heat pumps meet low-temperature industrial heat with a fraction of the electricity, sparing the grid new capacity.

Cost, confidence and supply hold the market back: high upfront cost, efficiency claims tested under foreign standards, and dependence on Chinese imports; Indian standards, BIS certification and a star label should come before demand surges.
GS3 · Industrial policy / GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Standards and labels before a demand surge, plus domestic manufacturing, keep electrification from importing new dependencies.

title: Steel policy for 2047 needs to shift focus — from protection to competition
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Montek S Ahluwalia, Shishir Gupta & Rishita Sachdeva, CSEP)
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effect on growth; Effects of liberalisation; Mineral resources · GS1 › Distribution of industries and mineral resources; Effects of globalisation · GS2 › Government policies
summary: On the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047, the writers argue Indian steel is profitable because it is protected, not efficient, and that duties, quality-control orders and the iron-ore export duty must be phased down.
ideas: Big but not yet competitive: India has risen to the world's second-largest steel producer, but the draft policy's goal of global competitiveness needs a clear meaning, as high profits come from protection, not efficiency.
GS3 · Industrial policy
High profitability under protection is not the same as global competitiveness.
Cheap ore, underpaid states: a 30% export duty on high-grade iron ore keeps domestic ore far below global prices, subsidising steelmakers at the cost of mineral-rich regions and exploration.
GS3 · Mineral policy / GS1 · Resource regions
Export duties on ore transfer value from mineral-rich regions to steelmakers and discourage mining.
Protection hurts users of steel: import duties and Quality Control Orders make Indian steel costlier than even high-cost Japan, raising costs for construction, automobiles and export-oriented MSMEs.
GS3 · Industry / MSMEs
Protecting an input industry taxes every industry that uses it, especially MSME exporters.

Competition did not kill other industries: tariff cuts in pharmaceuticals and auto components were followed by rising shares in global exports; steel should cut duties to ASEAN levels over five years and drop QCOs.
GS3 · Liberalisation / Trade
Pharma and auto parts show that lower protection can raise, not reduce, export competitiveness.

Reform the structure, not just tariffs: consider privatising some public-sector plants, remove the ore export duty and overhaul mining policy that discourages exploration (explorers must surrender discovered mines to auction).
GS3 · PSU reform / Mining
Competitive steel needs privatisation of laggard PSUs and a mining policy that rewards exploration.
